Part 1

Simple Mediation — Practice

NSCAW/CPS Violence Study: Does PTSS mediate violence exposure → externalizing behaviour?

NSCAW Practice — Background & Research Questions
🔬 STUDY CONTEXT

I have longitudinal data from the NSCAW (National Survey of Child and Adolescent Well-Being) that has information about children who have been investigated by CPS for different types of abuse or neglect.

Let's test whether: (1) children who have witnessed severe violence at Wave 1 (EV_W1) are more likely to engage in externalizing behaviour at Wave 3 (bcext3); and (2) post-traumatic stress at Wave 1 (tra1) is the mechanism through which violence exposure is linked to externalizing behaviour.

📄 Full write-up on the course website

❓ HYPOTHESES
  • H1: Higher EV_W1 → more bcext3 at Wave 3
  • H2: tra1 (PTSS) mediates the link

N = 1,605 children investigated by CPS | Longitudinal across multiple waves

RoleVariableWhat It Measures
XEV_W1Violence exposure severity at Wave 1
Mtra1Traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) at Wave 1
Ybcext3Externalizing behaviour at Wave 3
EV_W1 (X)  →  tra1 (M)  →  bcext3 (Y)
🌍 WHY THIS MATTERS

If PTSS is the mechanism, trauma-focused therapy for CPS-involved children who witnessed violence could break the chain to behavioural problems.

The Simple Mediation Path Diagram

X affects Y directly AND indirectly through M

📖 READING THIS DIAGRAM

X affects Y in two ways simultaneously:

  • Directly — direct effect (c'): X→Y
  • Indirectly through M — X→M (a path) × M→Y (b path) = indirect effect (ab)
🔑 FUNDAMENTAL EQUATION

c = c′ + ab   (ALWAYS)

Total = Direct + Indirect. Check this in every output.

🔑 INDIRECT EFFECT SIGNIFICANCE

NEVER use p-values for indirect effects.
Use bootstrapped CIs.
CI excludes zero → ✅   CI includes zero → ❌

Step 1 — Does Violence Exposure Predict PTSS? (The 'a path')

PROCESS Model 4: Y=bcext3, X=EV_W1, M=tra1 | N=1,605

📖 WHAT WE'RE TESTING

The a path: Does violence exposure predict PTSS? First requirement for mediation.

📖 KEY RESULT: EV_W1 = 1.9423, p < .001 ✅

Every 1-unit increase in violence → PTSS rises 1.94 points. R²=.058.
a path confirmed ✅

🌍 REAL-LIFE MEANING

Children who witness more severe violence develop significantly more trauma symptoms. Violence causes PTSS — the theoretical foundation of this model.

⚠️ KEY DISTINCTION

When BOTH X and M are in the model, the X coefficient = direct effect (c'), NOT the total effect (c).

Step 2 — Do X and M Together Predict Externalizing? (b path + direct effect)

Both X and M in model → b path and direct effect c'

📖 WHAT WE'RE TESTING

b path: Does PTSS predict externalizing controlling for violence?
Direct c': Does violence still predict externalizing after controlling for PTSS?

📖 KEY RESULTS
  • EV_W1 (c') = 0.8237, p=.0003 ✅
  • tra1 (b) = 0.0976, p=.0005 ✅

Both pathways active — required for mediation.

🌍 REAL-LIFE MEANING

Violence retains a direct effect (c'=0.82) AND trauma also independently predicts acting-out (b=0.10). Both pathways are real.

Steps 3 & 4 — Total, Direct & Indirect Effects

Step 3: Total effect — ignoring the mediator

Step 4: Decomposed into direct + indirect

EffectValue95% Boot CI
Total (c)1.0133[0.58, 1.45]✅
Direct (c')0.8237[0.38, 1.27]✅
Indirect via PTSS0.1896[0.08, 0.31]✅ CI ≠ 0
✔️ MATHS CHECK

0.8237 + 0.1896 = 1.0133 ✔

🌍 CONFIRMED MEDIATOR

18.7% of total effect travels through trauma. Treating PTSS could reduce ~19% of downstream behavioural damage. Remaining 81% is direct — other mechanisms also exist.

Drawing Conclusions — NSCAW Violence Study
📊 THE BREAKDOWN
  • Total effect = 1.0133
  • Indirect via PTSS = 0.1896 → 18.71%
  • Direct = 0.8237 → 81.29%

PTSS is a partial mediator.

🔑 GOLDEN RULE

For indirect effects: bootstrapped CIs only.
CI excludes 0 → ✅   CI includes 0 → ❌

🌍 POLICY IMPLICATION

Traumatic symptoms are the mechanism linking violence exposure to externalizing problem behaviour among CPS-involved youth.

Dealing with the child's trauma from violence exposure can reduce long-term behavioural outcomes.

Treating PTSS is necessary but NOT sufficient — the 81% direct effect means other mechanisms (neurological, social learning, disrupted attachment) also need addressing.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGSimple Mediation — CPS Study

Total effect = 1.0133, indirect through PTSS = 0.1896. What is the direct effect?

A. 0.1896
B. 0.8237 — because c = c′ + ab → c′ = 1.0133 − 0.1896
C. 1.0133
D. Cannot calculate without more information
💡 HINT
Rearrange c = c′ + ab → c′ = c − ab.
✅ ANSWER

B. c′ = c − ab = 1.0133 − 0.1896 = 0.8237.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGInterpreting Mediation Results

The indirect effect through PTSS has a 95% bootstrap CI of [0.08, 0.31]. What do you conclude?

A. Not significant — need p < .05
B. Significant — CI does not include zero
C. Borderline — CI is wide
D. Cannot conclude from a CI alone
💡 HINT

✅ ANSWER

B. For indirect effects, use bootstrapped CIs only. CI [0.08, 0.31] excludes zero → significant.

Part 2

Adding Covariates to Mediation

Interpretation stays the same — just add 'controlling for C' throughout

Covariates in Mediation — The Statistical Equations

Equations with q covariates

Covariates enter model alongside X

📖 EQUATION 1 — PREDICTING M

M = iM + aX + f₁C₁ + … + fqCq + eM

a = a path. fi = covariate effect on M.

📖 EQUATION 2 — PREDICTING Y

Y = iY + c′X + bM + g₁C₁ + … + gqCq + eY

c′ = direct effect. b = b path.

📖 INTERPRETATION WITH COVARIATES

Direct (c′): Change in Y for 1-unit X, controlling for M and C.

Indirect (ab): X's effect through M, controlling for C.

c = c′ + ab — always. Covariates do NOT need to be in both equations.

Covariates — Why They Matter & PROCESS Options

Enable: Show total effect model + Standardized effects

🔬 WHY ADD COVARIATES?

Covariates rule out alternative explanations. By controlling for C, we ensure X→M→Y reflects the genuine mechanism, not confounding by additional factors.

Covariates do not need to be in both equations — include wherever theoretically relevant.

📖 KEY PROCESS OPTIONS
  • Show total effect model: prints c so you can verify c = c' + ab
  • Standardized effects: effect sizes in SD units
  • Pairwise contrasts: for multiple mediators

c = c′ + ab — always, with or without covariates.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGCovariates in Mediation

Must covariates be in BOTH the M equation AND the Y equation?

A. Yes — always in both
B. No — include wherever theoretically relevant; not required in both
C. Doesn't matter
D. Yes — otherwise c = c′ + ab breaks
💡 HINT
Where should a covariate go? Wherever it theoretically matters.
✅ ANSWER

B. Include wherever theoretically relevant. The interpretation stays the same — just hold C constant throughout.

Part 3

Economic Stress Study

ESTRESS → AFFECT → WITHDRAW — Mediation with 3 covariates (estress.sav)

Economic Stress Study — Background & Variables
🔬 STUDY CONTEXT

Participants were N=262 entrepreneurs who were members of Business Networking International, who responded to an online survey about their business performance and emotional reactions to the economic climate. (Pollack & Hayes)

Pollack and Hayes proposed that economic stress leads to depressed affect, which in turn enhances a business owner's intention to leave entrepreneurship. This is not a question about whether there is an effect, but HOW it operates.

❓ RESEARCH QUESTION

Does ESTRESS affect withdrawal intentions through depressed affect? Is AFFECT the mechanism?

ESTRESS (X)  →  AFFECT (M)  →  WITHDRAW (Y)
RoleVariableWhat It Measures
XESTRESSEconomic stress — how badly the business is doing
MAFFECTDepressed affect. Higher = more depressed.
YWITHDRAWWithdrawal intentions. Higher = more likely to quit.
C1ESEEntrepreneurial self-efficacy
C2SEXGender
C3TENUREYears in business
🔮 COVARIATE HYPOTHESES

ESE: More confidence → less depression → less withdrawal (negative expected)
TENURE: Direction genuinely unclear
SEX: No strong hypothesis — '?'

Example 3 — The Statistical Model with q=3 Covariates
📖 EQUATION 1 — AFFECT (M)

AFFECT = iM + a(ESTRESS) + f₁(ESE) + f₂(SEX) + f₃(TENURE) + eM

a path = effect of ESTRESS on AFFECT holding covariates constant.

📖 EQUATION 2 — WITHDRAW (Y)

WITHDRAW = iY + c′(ESTRESS) + b(AFFECT) + g₁(ESE) + g₂(SEX) + g₃(TENURE) + eY

c′ = direct effect after controlling for AFFECT and covariates.

⚠️ NOTE: Estimates will differ from simple mediation

Expected — covariates absorb variance previously attributed to X and M. Do not be alarmed.

c = c′ + ab — still holds always.

Example 3 — Statistical Path Diagram with All Covariates

Statistical path diagram: ESTRESS→AFFECT(a=0.159)→WITHDRAW; ESE(C1), SEX(C2), TENURE(C3) all included as covariates; b=0.707, c′=−0.094

Predictorβp

ese (f1)−0.1549.001✅
sex (f2)0.0148.863❌
tenure (f3)−0.0108.086❌ (trend)

R²=.163, F=12.52, p<.001 | Outcome: AFFECT

❓ HYPOTHESES CONFIRMED?

ESE → less depression ✅ confirmed
Tenure → unclear ✅ (marginal only)
Gender → no effect ✅

🌍 ESTRESS (a=0.159) ✅

Every 1-unit stress increase → +0.16 more depression, controlling for gender, confidence, and experience. a path confirmed.

🌍 ESE (β=−0.155) ✅

Higher self-efficacy → significantly LESS depression. Confident entrepreneurs cope better.

🌍 GENDER & TENURE

Gender not significant. Tenure shows only a marginal trend (p=.086).

AFFECT → WITHDRAW (b path + direct effect c′)
PredictorβpRole
affect (b path)0.7071<.001b path✅
estress (c′)−0.0935.077Direct❌
ese (g1)−0.2121.006Covariate✅
sex (g2)0.1274.378Covariate❌
tenure (g3)−0.0021.846Covariate❌

R²=.206, F=13.28, p<.001 | Outcome: WITHDRAW

🌍 AFFECT (b=0.707) ✅

Depression is a POWERFUL driver of quitting. Every 1-unit increase → 0.71 more withdrawal desire.

🌍 ESTRESS DIRECT (c′=−0.094) ❌

Once we control for depression, stress is NOT significantly related to withdrawal. The link works through mood.

🌍 ESE (g1=−0.212) ✅

Higher self-efficacy also directly reduces withdrawal (p=.006).

Indirect Effect — Does AFFECT Mediate Stress → Withdrawal?
EffectValue95% Boot CI
Total (c)0.0191[−.087, .126]❌
Direct (c′)−0.0935[−.197, .010]❌
Indirect via AFFECT0.1127[.057, .173]✅

c = c′ + ab → 0.019 ≈ −0.094 + 0.113 ✔

⚠️ SUPPRESSION PUZZLE

How can indirect be significant if total is NOT? Direct (−0.094) and indirect (+0.113) cancel each other out, making the total near zero. The mediated path is real — this is a suppression effect.

🌍 MEDIATION CONFIRMED ✅

Stress → withdrawal ONLY through depression. The path: stress → depression → wanting to quit.

💡 INTERVENTION IMPLICATION

To reduce business owner burnout: treat the depression. Reducing stress alone may not reduce dropout rates.

📊 EFFECT SIZE

Standardized indirect = 0.1518 (~1/7th of a SD). Modest but real and actionable.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGEconomic Stress — Suppression Effect

Total = 0.019 (n.s.). Indirect = 0.113 (sig.). How is this possible?

A. Statistical error — cannot happen
B. Direct is negative (−0.094), cancelling the positive indirect (+0.113)
C. Indirect is always larger than total
D. The CI must be wrong
💡 HINT
c = c′ + ab. If c=0.019 and ab=0.113, what must c′ be?
✅ ANSWER

B. Suppression: −0.094 + 0.113 ≈ 0.019. c = c′ + ab always holds.

Part 4

Parallel Mediation — Model 4

Multiple independent mediators: The PMI Sugar Study (Example 4)

Why Simple Mediation Isn't Always Enough
⚠️ THE PROBLEM

Simple mediation assumes X influences Y through only one mediator. In reality, most effects operate through multiple pathways simultaneously.

Multiple Mechanisms Exist

The effect of X on Y is rarely due to just one mediator — there are usually multiple contributing factors or pathways.

Mediators Can Be Mediated

A mediator (M) may itself be influenced by another mediator, creating a chain of effects rather than a simple direct link.

Misinterpretation of Direct Effect

The 'direct effect' (c′) might reflect the combined influence of multiple unmodelled mediators, not a truly direct pathway.

✅ USE PARALLEL (Model 4) WHEN:

Multiple mediators work independently. Each has its own separate path from X to Y. M1 and M2 do NOT influence each other.

X → M1 → Y
X → M2 → Y   (M1 and M2 independent)

✅ USE SERIAL (Model 6) WHEN:

Multiple mediators influence each other in sequence. X → M1 → M2 → Y.

📖 KEY RULES FOR PARALLEL

X exerts its effect through k + 1 pathways (1 direct + k indirect). Each indirect path = specific indirect effect.

c = c′ + Σ aᵢbᵢ   (always)

The Parallel Multiple Mediator Model — Theory & Formulas
📖 THE PARALLEL MODEL

Multiple mediators M₁, M₂, … Mᵢ operate independently — each transmits part of the effect of X on Y, but they do not influence each other.

The indirect effect through each Mᵢ = aᵢ × bᵢ, where aᵢ = X→Mᵢ and bᵢ = Mᵢ→Y, controlling for X and all other mediators.

📖 SPECIFIC INDIRECT EFFECTS

Each specific indirect effect reflects only the effect through Mᵢ, controlling for all other mediators and covariates. The model with k mediators has k specific indirect effects.

📐 THE FORMULAS

Specific indirect through Mᵢ = aᵢ × bᵢ

Total indirect = Σ aᵢbᵢ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … + aₖbₖ

c = c′ + Σ aᵢbᵢ   (always!)

With k=1: reduces to c = c′ + ab

📖 CONTROLLING FOR OTHER MEDIATORS

Since parallel mediators operate independently, the total indirect = the sum of all specific indirect effects.

The Parallel Multiple Mediator Model — Diagrams

Real example: 3 independent parallel mediators

General model for k parallel mediators

📐 KEY FORMULA

Total indirect = Σ aᵢbᵢ
c = c′ + Σ aᵢbᵢ   (always!)

The Parallel Multiple Mediator Model — Total Indirect Effect

Total indirect = Σ aᵢbᵢ  |  Total effect: c = c′ + Σ aᵢbᵢ

📖 WHEN ADDED TOGETHER

The specific indirect effects yield the total indirect effect of X on Y through all mediators.

Example with k=3: Total = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃

📐 THE KEY EQUATIONS

Total Indirect = Σ aᵢbᵢ

c = c′ + Σ aᵢbᵢ   (always!)

🔑 ALWAYS HOLDS

With 1, 2, or 10 mediators — total = direct + ALL specific indirect effects. If numbers don't add up, check your model.

Sugar Study — Full Background, Variables & Research Question
🔬 STUDY CONTEXT

N=123 Israelis (43 male, 80 female) read an article about a potential sugar shortage. Half (n=58) were told it would appear on the FRONT PAGE of a major newspaper; half (n=65) were told it was in the MIDDLE OF AN ECONOMIC SUPPLEMENT. Same article — only described placement differed.

Participants reported their intention to buy sugar (REACTION) and their belief that others would be influenced by the media (PMI).

❓ RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS

Front-page placement doesn't directly drive buying. It works through two psychological mechanisms:

  1. IMPORT: 'Front page = this shortage must be serious'
  2. PMI: 'Everyone will panic-buy — I should too' (bandwagon)
RoleVariableWhat It Measures
XCOND1=front page, 0=interior
M1IMPORTPerceived importance of the article
M2PMIPresumed media influence — belief others will be influenced
YREACTIONIntention to buy sugar
COND (X)  →  IMPORT (M1)  →  REACTION (Y)
COND (X)  →  PMI (M2)    →  REACTION (Y)
Interpreting the Mediation Effect — Two Ways

Two ways to interpret the mediation effect — Hayes textbook style vs plain English (GEBS)

Parallel Mediation — M Equation Outputs (PMI and IMPORT)
📖 PMI (M2): a2 = 0.4765, p=.0454 ✅

Front-page placement significantly increases presumed media influence. 'Everyone will be influenced by this.'

📖 IMPORT (M1): a1 = 0.6268, p=.0452 ✅

Front-page placement significantly increases perceived importance. 'This shortage must be serious.'

⚠️ SAME AS SINGLE MEDIATION MODEL

These estimates are the same as the single mediation model. The M equations are unchanged regardless of how many mediators you add. The difference shows up only in the Y equation and indirect effects.

🌍 BOTH a PATHS CONFIRMED ✅

Both psychological mechanisms are activated by front-page placement. First requirement for parallel mediation met.

Parallel Mediation — M Equation PROCESS Output (PMI and IMPORT)

PROCESS output for both M equations — note: same estimates as single mediation model

Parallel Mediation — Y Equation (REACTION)

PROCESS output: Y equation | R²=.3251, F=19.11, p<.001

📖 READING THE OUTPUT

cond (c′) = 0.1034, p=.666 ❌
Article placement does NOT directly affect buying.

pmi (b2) = 0.3965, p < .001 ✅

import (b1) = 0.3244, p < .001 ✅

🌍 THE PSYCHOLOGICAL MECHANISMS DO ALL THE WORK

The direct effect is non-significant. Seeing the front-page headline does NOT directly make you want to buy sugar. It works entirely THROUGH the psychological mediators.

Parallel Mediation — Direct Effect of X on Y

Direct effect output from PROCESS

📖 READING THE OUTPUT

Direct effect (c′) = 0.1034, p = .6662, CI [−.3701, .5768]

The CI includes zero → not significant.

🌍 WHAT THIS MEANS

The direct effect of being told the article would be published on the front page (X) on the intention to buy sugar (Y) is small and non-significant (p > 0.05).

The confidence interval includes zero, meaning there is no evidence of a direct effect of article position on purchase intention. All effect works indirectly through the psychological mediators.

Parallel Mediation — Indirect Effects of X on Y

Indirect effects output with full interpretation table

📖 KEY RESULTS

TOTAL = 0.3923, CI [.0814, .7233] ✅
Overall mediation is significant.

PMI = 0.1890, CI [−.0009, .4071] ⚠️
Borderline — CI barely includes zero.

IMPORT = 0.2033, CI [.0021, .4424] ✅
Significant — CI excludes zero.

🔑 RULE

Bootstrapped CIs only.
CI excludes 0 → ✅   CI includes 0 → ❌

Interpreting the Indirect Effects — The Full Calculation

Interpreting the Indirect Effects

📖 TOTAL INDIRECT (0.392)

People in the front-page condition had an intention to buy sugar that was 0.392 units higher due to the article's influence on the mediators, which in turn affected their purchase intention.

🌍 PMI (0.189) & IMPORT (0.203)

PMI: 0.189 units higher because placement influenced their perception of media importance, which affected purchase intention.
IMPORT: 0.203 units higher due to its influence on their perception of article importance, which shaped their intention to purchase sugar.

Sugar Study — Statistical Diagram with All Coefficients

All path coefficients from the parallel mediation model

📖 THE COEFFICIENTS
  • a1=0.627: front page → more perceived importance
  • a2=0.477: front page → more PMI
  • b1=0.324: importance → more buying
  • b2=0.397: PMI → more buying
  • c'=0.103: direct (NOT significant)
📐 CALCULATE

Indirect IMPORT: 0.627×0.324 = 0.203 ✅
Indirect PMI: 0.477×0.397 = 0.189 ⚠️
Direct: 0.103 ❌

0.103+0.203+0.189 = 0.495 ≈ total ✔

Simple vs. Parallel Mediation — Published CPA Example

Fig. 2: Simple mediation — all bonds combined

Fig. 3: Parallel mediation — three separate pathways

🌍 WHY PARALLEL IS MORE INFORMATIVE

Parallel reveals engagement (M1) and academic outcomes (M3) are significant mediators, but connectedness (M2) is NOT. This precision shapes what school-based interventions would actually work to reduce adult violence.

Part 5

Serial Mediation — Model 6

What if the mediators cause each other? Testing X → M1 → M2 → Y

Serial Mediation — Definition & Key Concepts
📖 WHAT IS SERIAL MEDIATION?

Serial mediation rejects the assumption that mediators are independent — instead, it models causal relationships between mediators.

X first influences M1, which then affects M2, and so on, ultimately influencing Y. The goal is to model a stepwise causal process.

🌍 SCHOOL BONDING EXAMPLE

Parallel: school attachment (M1) and academic achievement (M2) independently mediate CPA → violence.

Serial: child maltreatment reduces school attachment (M1), which then lowers academic achievement (M2), ultimately influencing bad outcomes (Y). M1 CAUSES M2.

📖 THE SERIAL CHAIN

X → M1 → M2 → Y

FeatureParallel (M4)Serial (M6)
M's cause each other?❌ No✅ Yes
Order matters?❌ No✅ Critical
New unique path?NoneX→M1→M2→Y
PROCESS model46
🔑 THE NEW PATH: Ind3 = a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂

d₂₁ = the M1→M2 coefficient. ONLY exists in serial mediation. Cannot be tested with parallel (Model 4).

Key Differences Between Serial and Parallel Mediation
📖 WHAT THEY SHARE

In both models, the total effect of X on Y is partitioned into direct and indirect effects. Part of X's influence occurs directly, part indirectly through mediators.

Regression weights represent the strength of relationships at each step. These coefficients estimate the expected difference in Y for a one-unit change in X, as it propagates through the mediators.

📖 WHAT MAKES SERIAL DIFFERENT
  • Mediators influence each other in a causal sequence
  • The order of mediators matters — entry order defines your causal hypothesis
  • Total indirect includes the chain path: X→M1→M2→Y (Ind3)
  • Serial = Model 6 | Parallel = Model 4
EffectParallelSerial
Total = direct + indirect✅ Yes✅ Yes
Order of M's matters❌ No✅ Yes
Ind3 = a₁×d₂₁×b₂❌ No✅ Yes
M's independent✅ Yes❌ No
📐 THREE INDIRECT EFFECTS (2 mediators)

Ind1: X→M1→Y = a₁ × b₁
Ind2: X→M2→Y = a₂ × b₂
Ind3 (NEW!): X→M1→M2→Y = a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂

🔑 THEORY DRIVES THE CHOICE

M1 causes M2 → serial (Model 6).
M1 and M2 independent → parallel (Model 4).

Child Maltreatment, School Bonds & Adult Violence: A Serial Mediation Model

Fig. 1: Theoretical model — the serial cascade from abuse to adult violence

📊 HYPOTHESIS 1

Physically abused children will have lower school connectedness, engagement, and achievement, and will be more likely to persist in violent behaviour as adults (direct effect between CPA and adult violence).

📊 HYPOTHESIS 2

School characteristics will both independently, jointly, and serially mediate the relationship between CPA and persistence in adult violence.

📊 HYPOTHESIS 3

Gender will moderate the mediation effect of school characteristics on the CPA → adult violence relationship.

Two-Mediator Serial Model — Statistical Diagram

Statistical diagram: d21 = M1→M2 arrow — the defining feature of serial mediation

Two-Mediator Serial Model — Conceptual & Statistical Diagrams

Conceptual + statistical diagrams with formulas: Ind1=a1b1; Ind3=a1·d21·b2

📖 THREE INDIRECT EFFECTS

Ind1: X→M1→Y = a₁ × b₁
Ind2: X→M2→Y = a₂ × b₂
Ind3 (NEW!): X→M1→M2→Y = a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂

🔑 IND3 IS THE NEW PATH

Ind3 = a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂ captures the COMPLETE SERIAL CHAIN: X → M1 → M2 → Y. This path can ONLY be tested with serial mediation (Model 6). It is the unique contribution of the serial model.

📖 WHAT d₂₁ MEANS

d₂₁ is the coefficient on the M1→M2 arrow. It estimates how much M1 influences M2. Without this path you have parallel mediation. With it tested, you have serial.

Simple vs. Serial Mediation — CPA Published Example

Simple mediation (limited)

Fig. 4: Serial model — M1→M2→M3 chain revealed

📖 WHAT THE SERIAL MODEL ADDS

The serial model adds d21=.503*** — school engagement significantly predicts connectedness. That cascade is the theoretical mechanism. Parallel mediation would miss it entirely.

Take the Output ONE Step at a Time!
📋 THE FOUR STEPS
  1. Step 1: Does X → IMPORT (M1)? Check a1 and CI.
  2. Step 2: Does IMPORT → PMI (d21)? Does X still predict PMI (a2)?
  3. Step 3: Do IMPORT and PMI → REACTION? Check b1, b2, and c′.
  4. Step 4: Examine Ind1, Ind2, Ind3 and contrast tests.
🔑 MODEL 6 SETUP

Enter mediators in causal order — IMPORT first (M1), PMI second (M2). Order is critical! Reversing tests a completely different theory.

Serial Model Results — Statistical Diagram with Coefficients

d21=0.196, p=.004 *** — the serial chain is confirmed

STEP 1: COND → IMPORT (a1=0.627, p=.045) ✅

Front-page placement significantly increases perceived importance.

STEP 2: IMPORT → PMI (d21) — THE SERIAL LINK

a2 (COND→PMI directly): β=0.354, p=.131 ❌ Not significant once IMPORT included.

d21 (IMPORT→PMI): β=0.196, p=.004 ✅ The serial chain is confirmed!

STEP 3: Both → REACTION

b1(IMPORT)=0.324*** ✅   b2(PMI)=0.397*** ✅
c′(COND direct)=0.103, p=.666 ❌

Serial Mediation — Three Indirect Effects (Step 4)
PathFormulaEffect95% CI
Total indirect0.392[.084, .733]✅
Ind1: COND→IMPORT→Ya₁×b₁0.203[.000, .453]✅
Ind2: COND→PMI→Ya₂×b₂0.140[−.050, .350]❌
Ind3: COND→IMPORT→PMI→Ya₁×d₂₁×b₂0.049[−.000, .137]⚠️
📖 Ind3 = 0.627 × 0.196 × 0.397 = 0.049

Borderline with N=123. This is the unique finding only serial mediation can test.

🌍 Ind1 ✅: 'This is serious' → buy sugar

Front page → perceived importance → buying. Confirmed.

🌍 Ind2 ❌: PMI alone doesn't hold up

Not a significant standalone pathway when serial structure is modelled.

🌍 Ind3 ⚠️: THE SERIAL CHAIN

Front page → importance → bandwagon → buy sugar. Full cascade exists. Borderline due to small N. Theoretically the most interesting finding.

📊 CONTRASTS: No pathway is significantly stronger

All contrast CIs include 0. Bigger numbers ≠ significantly different effects.

Contrast Tests & Combining Parallel + Serial Models

Enable 'Pairwise contrasts of indirect effects' in PROCESS options

ContrastComparisonDiff.95% CI
C1Ind1 − Ind20.063[−.231, .390]
C2Ind1 − Ind30.155[−.004, .383]
C3Ind2 − Ind30.092[−.121, .322]
📖 RESULT: ALL CIs INCLUDE ZERO

No pathway is significantly stronger than another. With N=123, not enough power to detect pathway differences. Bigger numbers ≠ significantly different effects.

📖 WHAT CONTRASTS TEST

Is one indirect pathway significantly stronger than another? Just because Ind1 (0.203) looks bigger than Ind3 (0.049) numerically doesn't mean it's statistically stronger.

You need to run the pairwise contrast tests and check whether the difference CI excludes zero before concluding one mediator is stronger.

🔑 KEY LESSON

Always use confidence intervals to compare indirect effects, never raw estimates alone.

See next slide for combining parallel + serial models (Model 81).

Combining Parallel + Serial Models — Model 81

Model 81: Model A (M1 serial with M2+M3 parallel) and Model B (M1/M2/M3 parallel feeding M4 serially)

🔑 MODEL 81

PROCESS can estimate models with BOTH parallel AND serial mediators simultaneously.

Model A: M1 is serial with M2, but M2 and M3 are parallel to each other.

Model B: M1/M2/M3 all parallel, all feed into M4 serially.

Look through the dozens of options in the Hayes book appendix for the right configuration for your theory.

💡 THE POINT

Mediation doesn't have to be purely parallel OR purely serial. Real theoretical models are often combinations — and PROCESS has pre-programmed templates for dozens of configurations.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGSerial Mediation — The New Path

A. a₁ × b₁
B. a₁ × b₂
C. a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂ — X to M1, M1 to M2, M2 to Y
D. a₂ × b₂

✅ ANSWER

C. Ind3 = a₁ × d₂₁ × b₂. d₂₁ is the M1→M2 coefficient — only in serial mediation.

Part 6

Simple Moderation — Model 1

PTSS × Sexual minority status → Delinquency

What Is Moderation? The Two Diagrams

Conceptual: W modifies the X→Y relationship

Statistical: XW interaction term is the test

📖 READING THE DIAGRAMS

Conceptual: W 'sits on' the X→Y arrow — modifies its strength or direction.

Statistical: We add XW (X × W, mean-centred) to regression. b₃ on XW IS the formal test.

Ŷ = i + b₁(X) + b₂(W) + b₃(X×W)

If b₃ is significant → MODERATION CONFIRMED.

🌍 MODERATION vs MEDIATION

Mediation: HOW does X affect Y? (mechanism)
Moderation: FOR WHOM or WHEN does X affect Y? (condition)

🔑 THE ONLY TEST

The ONLY test of moderation is the significance of b₃ (the interaction term). A non-significant main effect of W (b₂) does NOT mean W is not a moderator.

Example 7 — Study Context, Variables & PROCESS Setup
🔬 STUDY CONTEXT

Data from youth in the child welfare system. We know PTSS predicts delinquency — but equally for ALL youth?

Sexual minority (LGBTQ+) youth face unique stressors NOT experienced by heterosexual youth: discrimination, family rejection, victimisation by peers, and less access to affirming support. These may amplify how trauma translates into delinquent behaviour.

❓ HYPOTHESIS

b₃ (ptss × sexmin) will be positive and significant — trauma more strongly linked to delinquency for LGBTQ+ youth.

RoleVariableMeasures
XptssPost-traumatic stress symptoms
Wsexmin1=LGBTQ+, 0=heterosexual
YdelinqDelinquent behaviour score

PROCESS setup: Model 1, Y=delinq, X=ptss, W=sexmin

Moderation — PROCESS Options Setup

Key options: visualisation code + J-N output + mean centring

📖 KEY OPTIONS TO ENABLE
  • Generate code for visualising: PROCESS outputs syntax to create the interaction plot — ALWAYS enable this.
  • Mean center: only continuous variables: reduces multicollinearity between X and XW.
  • Johnson-Neyman output: for continuous moderators — gives the exact threshold.
  • Conditioning values: 16th, 50th, 84th percentiles for the plot.
🔑 WHEN TO USE J-N

With a continuous moderator (like age), J-N gives the exact threshold — far more informative than just 3 percentile values. See Part 7.

Moderation Results — Output & Equations
PredictorCoeffSEp
constant1.7075.263<.001—
ptss (main)−0.0450.062.467❌
sexmin (main)1.7454.529.001✅
ptss × sexmin (Int_1)0.2579.125.040✅ MODERATION!

R²=.141, F=6.60, p=.0004

📖 THE TWO EQUATIONS

Heterosexual (W=0):
Ŷ = 1.71 + (−0.045)(ptss) — flat, not sig

LGBTQ+ (W=1):
Ŷ = 3.455 + (0.213)(ptss) — positive, rising

b₃ = 0.258 IS the difference in slopes between the two groups.

🌍 REAL-LIFE MEANING

Moderation confirmed (b₃=0.2579, p=.040).

Heterosexual youth: PTSS does NOT significantly predict delinquency.

LGBTQ+ youth: Higher PTSS → more delinquency. Trauma uniquely externalises as delinquent behaviour for sexual minority youth.

Policy implication: Trauma-informed delinquency prevention must SPECIFICALLY target sexual minority youth. Universal programmes may be insufficient.

Model WITHOUT Interaction — Parallel Slopes: Dummy Variable Shifts Intercept Up

Ŷ = 1.71 − 0.045(ptss) + 1.745(sexmin) — No interaction term

📖 WHAT THIS SHOWS

Without an interaction term, the two lines are perfectly parallel — identical slopes, shifted vertically. The dummy variable b₂ = +1.745 lifts the sexual minority line up by 1.745 units at EVERY value of PTSS.

📐 THE TWO EQUATIONS

Heterosexual (sexmin=0):
Ŷ = 1.71 + (−0.045)(ptss)

Sexual minority (sexmin=1):
Ŷ = 1.71 + 1.745 + (−0.045)(ptss) = 3.455 + (−0.045)(ptss)

🔑 KEY POINT

Parallel slopes = effect of PTSS on delinquency is IDENTICAL for both groups. Only baseline differs. This is the null hypothesis — no moderation.

Model WITH Interaction — Diverging Slopes: PTSS Has a Stronger Effect for Sexual Minority Youth

Ŷ = 1.71 − 0.045(ptss) + 1.745(sexmin) + 0.258(ptss×sexmin)

📖 WHAT THIS SHOWS

Adding b₃ = +0.258 changes the slope for sexual minority youth. Lines DIVERGE — gap widens as PTSS increases.

📐 THE SLOPE CHANGE

Heterosexual slope: −0.045 (flat)
Sexual minority slope:
−0.045 + 0.258 = +0.213 (rising)

b₃ = 0.258 IS the difference in slopes (p=.040 ✅)

🌍 REAL-LIFE MEANING

Heterosexual youth: more trauma → slightly less delinquency (not significant).
LGBTQ+ youth: more trauma → significantly more delinquency. Trauma externalises for this group.

Side-by-Side Comparison — No Interaction vs With Interaction

❌ NO INTERACTION

Both slopes = −0.045. Dummy shifts intercept UP by +1.745. Lines perfectly parallel.

✅ WITH INTERACTION (b₃=0.258, p=.040)

Hetero slope = −0.045 | Sexmin slope = +0.213. Lines diverge → MODERATION.

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGSimple Moderation — Identifying the Test

Output: b1(stress)=0.45, p=.001; b2(gender)=0.12, p=.34; b3(stress×gender)=0.31, p=.08. What is concluded?

A. Moderation confirmed — b₃ is close to significance
B. Moderation NOT confirmed — b₃ (p=.08) is not significant at .05
C. Gender not a moderator because b₂ is non-significant
D. Stress is the only significant predictor
💡 HINT
What specifically tests moderation?
✅ ANSWER

B. The ONLY test of moderation is b₃ (the interaction). p=.08 does not reach p<.05. Non-significance of b₂ is irrelevant.

Homework (X) → grades (Y): b=0.8 for high-motivation (W=1), b=0.1 for low-motivation (W=0). Interaction significant. What does this mean?

A. Motivation causes homework — it's a mediator
B. The effect of homework on grades DEPENDS ON motivation level
C. Homework has zero effect on low-motivation students
D. Motivation should be removed as a confounder

Is motivation IN the causal path (mediation) or does it CHANGE the X→Y slope (moderation)?

Johnson-Neyman Technique

Finding the exact value of W where the effect becomes statistically significant

Age as Continuous Moderator — PROCESS Setup & Options

Model 1: Y=bcdel1, X=tra1, W=ageY | N=1,910

Key options: J-N output ✓ | Generate code ✓ | Percentiles

📖 WHY J-N?

With a continuous moderator (age), J-N gives the exact value of W where the conditional effect crosses p=.05. Far more informative than just 3 percentile snapshots.

J-N Full PROCESS Output — Complete Output

Full PROCESS output: Model 1, Y=bcdel1, X=tra1, W=ageY | Interaction confirmed Int_1=0.0222, p=.016 | Conditional effects at ages 9, 11, 14

J-N Full PROCESS Output — Reading the Results
📖 INTERACTION: Int_1=0.0222, p=.016 ✅

PTSS × age interaction is statistically significant! R²-change=.003, F=5.768, p=.016. Moderation is confirmed — age changes the PTSS→delinquency relationship.

📖 CONDITIONAL EFFECTS AT THREE AGES
Age (percentile)Effect of PTSSpSig?
9 (16th)0.0713.006✅
11 (50th)0.1156<.001✅
14 (84th)0.1821<.001✅
🌍 WHAT THE PERCENTILES SHOW

The effect of PTSS on delinquency GROWS with age:

β=0.071 at age 9 → β=0.116 at age 11 → β=0.182 at age 14

J-N will tell us exactly where it first becomes significant — see the full output on the previous slide.

⚠️ WHERE DOES IT BECOME SIGNIFICANT?

The percentile values show the effect is significant at ages 9, 11, and 14. But what about children aged 8? 7?

The J-N technique (next slide) gives us the exact threshold.

Johnson-Neyman Significance Region

J-N threshold: age 8.43 — 86% of sample above this

📖 LINE-BY-LINE READING

Threshold=8.4253: PTSS effect becomes significant at age 8.43.

13.82% below: 13.8% of children young enough that effect is NOT significant.

86.18% above: large majority — PTSS significantly predicts delinquency.

Age 8.0: CI includes 0 → not sig.
Age 8.43: exactly p=.05.
Age 9.5+: all CIs exclude 0.

🌍 REAL-LIFE MEANING

PTSS starts predicting delinquency at ~age 8.5. For younger children, trauma may manifest as internalising (anxiety, depression). For older children it externalises as delinquency.

Screen for PTSS-delinquency links especially in children aged 9+.

Moderation Plot — Age × PTSS → Delinquency

Diverging lines confirm moderation visually

📖 HOW TO READ THIS GRAPH
  • All lines slope UP: higher PTSS = more delinquency for all ages
  • Lines DIVERGE (not parallel): this IS moderation
  • Age 14 (gray): highest baseline AND steepest slope
  • Age 9 (blue): lowest baseline AND flattest slope

Parallel lines → NO moderation
Diverging lines → MODERATION ✅

PROCESS outputs this syntax automatically

🎯 CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDINGJohnson-Neyman Technique

J-N output: threshold = 8.43 years, 86.18% of sample above. What does this mean?

A. Only 13.82% show a significant moderation effect
B. PTSS→delinquency effect is significant for children aged 8.43 and above (86.18%)
C. Children must be ≥8.43 to be included in PROCESS
D. The model explains 86.18% of variance
💡 HINT
What does 'region of significance' mean?
✅ ANSWER

B. The J-N threshold is the age at which the conditional effect crosses p=.05. For 86.18% of children (age ≥8.43), the effect is significant. For younger children (13.82%), it is not.

Quick Reference — Golden Rules & Model Selection
Research QuestionPROCESS ModelKey Feature
Does W change the X→Y effect?Model 1Tests XW interaction (b₃). Use J-N for continuous W.
X→Y through one MModel 4a, b, c′, indirect via bootstrapped CI
X→Y through multiple independent M'sModel 4Specific indirect effects. Contrasts. c=c′+Σaibi.
Mediators cause each otherModel 6d₂₁ path; Ind3=a₁×d₂₁×b₂; order matters!
Parallel + serial combinedModel 81Check Hayes book appendix
🔑 FOUR GOLDEN RULES

Rule 1: c = c′ + ab always. Total = direct + all indirect effects.

Rule 2: Indirect effects → bootstrapped CIs only. CI excludes 0 ✅ / CI includes 0 ❌.

Rule 3: Moderation = non-parallel lines. b₃ on XW is the statistical test.

Rule 4: Serial → order of M's defines your causal hypothesis. Theory drives the model.
